result.summary: Pausanias continues his tour of the athlete statues at Olympia, focusing on the Rhodian family of Diagoras, whose sons and grandsons won many boxing and pancratium crowns. He recounts Dorieus's career and death, then lists other boxers and runners, including Dromeus, said to have introduced a meat diet.

scenes.title: Diagoras and his family's statues
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes the statues of Diagoras, his sons and grandsons, and tells how his sons carried him on their shoulders amid flowers.

scenes.title: Dorieus: exile, capture and death
scenes.summary: Pausanias gives the descent of Diagoras and recounts Dorieus's victories, exile to Thurii, capture by Athens and execution by Sparta according to Androtion.
scenes.stakes: Dorieus risks punishment by Athens as an enemy captive, and later execution by Sparta.

scenes.title: More boxers and runners
scenes.summary: Pausanias lists further statues: Alcænetus and sons, Gnatho, Lycinus, Dromeus and Pythocles, with their sculptors.

notable_quotes.reason: Vivid image of Diagoras carried on his sons' shoulders and showered with flowers.
Credits Dromeus with introducing meat into athletes' training diet.

analysis.text: Pausanias uses statues as a guide to family achievement and civic pride, showing athletic glory passing through generations, even through daughters' sons.
Dorieus's fate reflects the Peloponnesian and Corinthian wars, when Greek states switched alliances and treated famous captives unpredictably.

legacy.text: Diagoras's triumph, carried by his sons, became a classical ideal of fortunate parenthood; the story is often repeated in later writers and is the source of the phrase 'Die, Diagoras, for you will not ascend to Olympus'.

fun_facts.text: The story of Pisirodus's mother disguised as a trainer is one of several tales explaining why Olympic trainers later had to attend unclothed.

language_notes.text: Pancratium was a brutal combined contest of wrestling and boxing, with very few rules.
"Against all comers" means he won the open contest, apparently without being matched against a set opponent.
"Practised as boxers" means they trained and competed as boxers; Pisirodus's mother smuggled him in disguised, since women were barred from watching.
Winning "without a contest" means no rival dared to face him, so he took the crown unopposed.
"Entered as Thurians" means they were officially announced as citizens of Thurii, not Rhodes.
Conon, an Athenian admiral serving the Persian king, helped bring about Rhodes's revolt from Sparta around 395 BC.
Thrasyllus was one of the generals at Arginusæ (406 BC), executed by Athens after the battle in a rash, unjust trial.
Athletes' diet: before Dromeus, trainers fed athletes mainly cheese rather than meat.

context_notes.text: Olympia's Altis was the sacred grove where victor statues stood; Diagoras's family was among the most famous Olympic dynasties.
Aristomenes was the legendary Messenian hero of the wars against Sparta.
Thurii was a colony in southern Italy founded in 444 BC under Athenian leadership.
The pentathlum was a five-event contest including running, jumping, discus, javelin and wrestling.

literary_notes.text: The picture of sons carrying their father beneath a shower of flowers vividly captures a father's peak of glory.
The Athenians arrive angry and threatening, yet the sight of the famous captive disarms them, reversing expectation.
Pausanias closes the digression with a summary judgment, marking a transition back to listing statues.
